data.title: Green SM Starts Amsterdam Taxi Pilot, Bringing the Green EV to Europe
data.description:
AMSTERDAM — Vietnamese electric mobility company Green SM began a pilot electric taxi service in Amsterdam on Thursday, making the Netherlands its second European market after Denmark and extending the commercial use of VinFast vehicles in a market where the automaker established a presence four years ago.

Green SM will initially operate in Amsterdam’s Centrum, West and Zuid districts before expanding to Oost, Noord, Nieuw-West and Zuidoost. The company said the pilot will be used to build its driver network, refine operations and establish service standards before expanding across the Dutch capital.

The Amsterdam operation adds another layer to a European expansion that began with VinFast in 2022. VinFast made its European market debut at EVS35 in Oslo in June that year with the VF 8 and VF 9, followed by a Dutch debut at EV Experience at Circuit Zandvoort in September. In October 2022, the company announced Amsterdam as its Netherlands headquarters and planned a local retail operation. Its first two European stores opened in Cologne, Germany, and Paris in December 2022.

By October 2025, Amsterdam was already part of VinFast’s European infrastructure. The company exhibited its EB 8 and EB 12 electric buses at Busworld Europe in Brussels, where the EB 12 was presented as a European-compliant model. VinFast identified the Netherlands and Belgium among its initial European target markets for the electric-bus business. Busworld also described the event as VinFast’s European debut for its electric buses.

The timing is significant because Green SM is not a separate vehicle manufacturer. The company, established in Vietnam in 2023, operates an electric mobility service built around VinFast vehicles. Reuters reported earlier this month that Green SM planned to enter the Netherlands and other European markets as part of its international expansion.

Green SM began European operations in Copenhagen in July, making Denmark its first European market. The Netherlands is now its eighth market globally, according to the company.

The Amsterdam operation uses an integrated model in which Green SM supplies the electric vehicles and operates the mobility platform while building its own driver network. In the Netherlands, the company is offering both employment and vehicle-rental arrangements. Drivers using the rental model can receive up to 85% of trip revenue, according to Green SM.

Richard Nabil Chahine, CEO of Green SM Europe, said the company’s immediate priority was to establish a reliable operation and adapt its service to the Dutch market.

“The Netherlands is an important next step in Green SM’s journey in Europe,” Chahine said in the company’s announcement. He said the company would use feedback from customers and drivers to refine the service.

Green SM is offering introductory discounts of 50% per trip, capped at 30 euros, for up to 10 rides per customer during the pilot. The company is also recruiting drivers in Amsterdam, where it has established a Dutch operating office.

The Amsterdam pilot gives VinFast another channel for putting its vehicles into commercial service in Europe while Green SM tests its electric taxi model in a market with an established electric-mobility sector. The company said the scale and coverage of its Amsterdam operation will be determined as the pilot progresses.

data.title: XPENG Grows in Malaysia, & Readies G9L for Global Launch
data.description:
Raymond just covered XPENG’s launch in the Philippines earlier today, but we also have news from the past week of the company expanding significantly in Malaysia and planning the launch of the G9L in 64 markets around the world. We’d love to see XPENG launch in the United States, but the fact is there’s much more growth potential elsewhere and the EV transition is booming in a bunch of other places while it stalls in the USA.

XPENG Setting Up Big Growth In Malasyia

First of all, a few days ago, we got the following news: “XPENG Malaysia today announced a major expansion of its nationwide retail and aftersales footprint, confirming 10 new strategic 3S/4S showroom locations targeted for deployment across Malaysia by the end of 2026. This rapid network development reinforces XPENG’s long-term commitment to establishing a comprehensive, high-touch Smart EV ownership ecosystem for Malaysian customers.”

We’ve heard it before with Tesla, Rivian, Lucid, and others — people want more than a sales location or an online ordering system before buying a new car; they want to make sure they can get service on the vehicle easily and efficiently when needed. That’s what the “3S/4S” thing is about. That means a “full 3S (Sales, Service & Spare Parts) or 4S (Sales, Service, Spare Parts, Body & Paint Services) facility.” That makes a big difference, and rolling out such centers in 10 new locations in Malaysia should significantly boost sales. “By embedding certified aftersales infrastructure, specialized diagnostic tools, and dedicated parts inventory directly into each site, XPENG ensures owners receive immediate, uncompromised long-term care from day one,” the company adds. “By embedding certified aftersales infrastructure, specialized diagnostic tools, and dedicated parts inventory directly into each site, XPENG ensures owners receive immediate, uncompromised long-term care from day one.” Sounds smart to me.

XPENG G9L Global Launch

XPENG’s new large, “next-gen” SUV, the G9L, is readying for a big global launch. It had its launch event a week ago for the Chinese auto market, but it will have a global launch on October 12 at the Paris Motor Show. (It will surely be in Malaysia before long.)

The company shares some key details about the SUV: “The G9L is XPENG’s Next-Gen AI Flagship SUV, available in both BEV and REEV versions. With an overall length of 5,120 mm and a wheelbase of 3,100 mm, the G9L features a golden wheelbase-to-length ratio of 0.605, delivering better space and handling agility than its segment peers. As a premium model, it embodies XPENG’s latest innovations in physical AI, spanning smart driving and the intelligent cockpit, and offering flagship-level features and global standards. Specifically, powered by the XPENG VLA 2.0 model, the G9L enables fast cross-region generalization, delivering a smooth, safe, and steady performance to more global markets. Meanwhile, the G9L features the same Turing AI chip as XPENG’s humanoid robot IRON.” Sounds compelling.

“The G9L meets the design standards of four major five-star safety ratings worldwide. It has completed 192 crash tests across four major protocols — Euro NCAP, ANCAP, C-NCAP, and CIASI — totaling more than 110 individual test items. Over a three-year period, it has also undergone global road testing across 26 countries and regions, with cumulative mileage surpassing 6.74 million kilometers. Its electric powertrain, engineered to global vehicle standards, delivers stability that stands up to extreme environments worldwide.”

I imagine the G9L will be a global hit for XPENG. We’ll have to check back in on it after it hits the airwaves again at the Paris Motor Show, and if it does end up seeing high consumer demand in markets around the world.

data.title: Donut Battery Vindicated: Element Analysis Proves Battery Not Lithium Or Sodium
data.description:
The latest release from Donut Lab’s “I Donut Believe” series is a surprise. Donut Lab has always used the proof series to puncture false claims and conspiracy theories. This one smashes lithium battery conspiracy theories. Truly, Ziroth is wrong. More and more, critics are clinging to falsehoods like cult followers drinking the Kool-Aid grasping at straws to create elaborate theories to justify falsehoods. One by one, critic theories are chopped down, and now another one is obliterated.

The analysis showed trace amounts of lithium and sodium at levels far below those in lithium or sodium batteries. Lithium and sodium are so abundant that they may be found in incidental amounts. There is not much to discuss here. What will it take for critics to realize they have been duped? When does Ziroth admit his conspiracy theory is wrong and his friend from Two Bit Da Vinci is right? This battery is definitively not lithium or sodium. Trying to prove it is either is futile.

Critics’ Cult-Like Following

Like all cults, the lithium conspiracy followers may persist past the point of rationality. There is little point in trying to convince them. No amount of reality will pop their self-fulfilling bubble. They need cult deprogramming. For Donut Lab, this video was a must. It had to extinguish a rumor that threatened its life. The conspiracy nuts will continue to weave new theories in a paroxysm of cognitive dissonance. The pain of admitting the truth will see to that. There is evidence the conspiracy theories are becoming ever more contrived and outlandish, to the point of irrationality. The theory that only one battery is not lithium and another actually is lithium is busted, but even without that, it shows critics contriving ever more preposterous and outlandish notions to justify their cloyish clinging to a fantasy to avoid painful truth.

While Donut Lab has more to prove, and can continue to do so, it becomes increasingly clear that critics are grasping at straws to justify themselves. They do not entertain pro and con or both sides of the analysis, but find every excuse to justify only one and not explain how another possibility exists. The evidence is pointing more and more toward Donut Lab presenting a cold sober reality, one that is a splash of cold water intended to wake dreamers from slumber. Grasping at a succession of failed guesses — a capacitor, an empty box, a hoax, a scam, red flags, there is no battery, a lithium battery, the test stopped at 90 degrees, a unique fingerprint voltage curve that was not unique, a bump theory — the list goes on. It is hard to keep track of all the crazy mistakes, errors, and false claims and expectations. It’s a hall of smoke and mirrors.

The Nonsense Needs to Stop

The world is experiencing levels of warming that are unprecedented. The crisis of global warming is urgent. We do not have time to waste time with irrational conspiracies and denier cults. If this battery technology has merit,
let it be used. So far, the evidence points to an important potential for pressing problems. Instead of using preconceived notions and prejudices, patience is needed. There are a host of innovations happening, spurred by recent global developments. Move on and make progress. Admit the truth. The truth is, new energy paradigms are emerging. There will be resistance.

data.title: Mazda 6e — Japanese Carmakers Fight Back in Australia
data.description:
At its launch into the Australian market eight months ago, the Mazda 6e received 2,000 pre-orders. It has delivered 693 of those cars in the last four months. I have long been an admirer of Mazda’s design, so we went to the local dealership to check it out. We were not disappointed. The Mazda 6e won the 2026 World Car of Year design award. In the back of my mind, I thought, perhaps this car might herald a resurgence of Japanese car sales in Australia.

Mazda produces just over 1 million cars per year, so it is not in the same league as Toyota, but it has a loyal niche following. Sales in Australia have been dropping this year, possibly because of model changeovers. Or could it be because of the increase in Chinese car sales?

For a bit of context, I checked out the sales figures of Japanese branded electric vehicles. So far in 2026, in the Australian market, Toyota has sold 2,523 EVs; Subaru — 1,277; Nissan — 219; Mazda — 693; and Suzuki — 40. This makes a total of 4,725. That’s similar to what one carmaker has sold with one model — the Tesla Model 3 (4,597). All Japanese EV sales approximately equal the Tesla Model 3’s sales. Japanese brands need to do better. The world needs them to participate meaningfully in the rEVolution. Your thoughts? (Dr Paul Wildman and myself have written extensively about this. See here.)

On Wednesday, we went to visit our local Mazda dealer on the north side of Brisbane to check out the latest offering. We met the Mazda 6e — designed by Mazda, built in China by Changan, based on its Deepal sub-brand. As we discovered, the interior design and exterior styling are pure Mazda. The underlying architecture is Deepal. You can read our article about the Deepal S07 here. The sales representative who generously gave us his time and expertise pointed out that even the stitching on the seats mirrored Mazda’s design DNA.

As we approached the dealership, we were impressed by the advertising for the 6e emblazoned over the entrance. The car on display was the PHEV version. We had to go around the back to see a car sitting ready for delivery, and three more examples. Bizarrely, a delivery of BT 50’s had been placed in front of the new Mazda 6e’s — making them difficult to see, and impossible to take for a test drive.

I was impressed by the value-for-money proposition when told the car was selling for only AU$54K. Apparently, this dealership alone is selling over a dozen a month, mainly to returning Mazda owners. The wife of our sales rep was driving the PHEV version. He was quite knowledgeable about his product and said he made it a point to know more about the vehicles he sells than his customers. He was well able to explain the apps needed for charging and the use of the supplied granny charger. An optional wall charger is available for purchase.

I did have a bone to pick with him when he kept giving charging times from zero. “You don’t run the battery down to zero,” I told him. However, the car comes with a 70 kWh LFP battery with 560 km of range, so it would be possible. Acceleration is a respectable zero to 100 km per hour in 7.6 seconds. Is that zoom, zoomy enough? The car is expected to be brought in for servicing every 20,000 km or 12 months, with a cost of about half the price of a petrol service. Over-the-air updates are available and can be installed at home.

As he explained the features of the car, I was struck by the fact that what used to be gimmicks or luxury items now come standard. For example: heated and cooled seats; 360-degree camera, accessed from the button steering wheel or voice commands. Also, but I didn’t mention this to him, it included a number of innovations that Tesla has debuted and caught a lot of flak for — the glass roof, the minimal dashboard, the large iPad-like screen, etc.

As I stood outside the car, chatting to the sales rep, Majella was busy inspecting the interior. The Mazda 6e comes with three different interior trims — beige, black, and tan — all at the same price. She said that it had the feeling of a sport model, with a smaller steering wheel. The Mazda 6e will be easy to spot on the road with its distinctive grille pattern.

As well as the main driving screen, there is a small screen behind the steering wheel and a heads-up display.

Egress is easy — with a clutch handle above the door and a proper silver door handle on the inside. The storage locker between the front seats is opened with a push button.

The latest scare tactic designed to stop Australian motorists from buying Chinese electric cars is to claim that they are a security risk. Your car is telling the Chinese Communist Party every time you go to Macca’s. Our helpful sales rep told us the amusing story of one customer who would not buy a Chinese brand because she was worried that it would be a security risk, so she bought a Mazda 6e. “But,” I said, “it’s made in China!” He shrugged his shoulders.

I asked Google about Australian government ministers owning and driving Chinese EVs and found out that Tony Burke, the Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister, personally owns a Chinese made electric vehicle. “Burke’s office stated that he informed his department and security agencies immediately upon appointment and followed security advice on appropriate precautions.”

Energy Minister Chris Bowen drives an XPENG G6 and points out that modern connected cars share data regardless of where they were made. Burke and Bowen have insisted that they have followed appropriate risk mitigation strategies, as advised by the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO). Cone of silence perhaps?

Some security concerns are valid. Both the USA and China have banned some connected vehicles from sensitive areas. Back in 2021, Teslas were banned from Chinese military sites. Is it a car or a surveillance tool? A data collector on wheels? Why aren’t people worried about their TVs, fridges, phones, etc. doing the same thing? I often think that my robot vacuum cleaner is conspiring with the intelligent fridge to take over the house.

With over 30 per cent of eligible parliamentary work vehicles being Chinese-built EVs (such as MG and BYD), ASIO has advised MPs and officials to exercise caution.

For those who wish to watch a video review of the Mazda 6e, check this out. This reviewer compares the Mazda 6e to the BYD Seal and the Tesla Model 3. Extra features include: V2L; remote controlled rear spoiler which can be set to be speed sensitive; handles present themselves by the use of the key fob. The reviewer describes it as old-world luxury, unlike Toyota’s EV offerings, but not at a luxury price. The electric roof screen (in two parts) can be opened from back controls. Lots of USB ports for all our modern devices. Wireless charging pad for the phone. Ambient lighting. And shortcut buttons on steering wheel.

The Mazda 6e even comes with a physical manual in the glovebox, sparking the reviewer to comment: “You can’t expect Japanese brands to be too advanced.” I am sure a lot of drivers would appreciate a physical manual, though.

Looking at the numbers, if Japanese carmakers wish to increase their EV penetration into the Australian market, they will have to massively increase the volume of cars available. The Mazda 6e, though a great value-for-money car, cannot do it alone. Exciting times as Australians get to drive beautifully designed Mazdas into an electric future.

data.title: XPENG Launches in the Philippines With Six EV Variants
data.description:
MANILA, Philippines — XPENG formally launched in the Philippines on Friday, September 25, with six variants of its L03 and X9, expanding its initial two-model offering to three battery-electric L03s, a range-extended version and two versions of the X9 electric MPV.

Attendees called the launch at the SM Mall of Asia Arena “the glitziest ever,” and brought XPENG Vice President for Finance and Accounting James Wu to Manila. Vincent Yambao, chief operating officer of XPENG Philippines joined actress and television host Anne Curtis, who was introduced as the brand’s Philippine ambassador on stage. About 3,000 guests attended the event, including dealers, banking partners, automotive executives, media and members of the public.

The L03 starts at ₱1.548 million (~$24,700) for the EV Standard Range and reaches ₱2.058 million (~$32,900) for the EV RWD Long Range Ultra.

The Standard Range uses a 58.3-kWh battery and has a claimed WLTP range of up to 445 kilometers. The L03 EV Long Range, priced at ₱1.698 million (~$27,100), uses a 71.1-kWh battery and is rated for up to 520 kilometers.

The L03 REEV sits between them at ₱1.598 million (~$25,500). Its 37.2-kWh battery provides up to 215 kilometers of electric driving. A gasoline engine serves as a generator rather than driving the wheels, giving the vehicle a combined WLTP range of up to 1,017 kilometers.

At ₱2.058 million (~$32,900), the L03 EV RWD Long Range Ultra uses the 71.1-kWh battery and adds more advanced driver-assistance and cabin equipment. Its claimed range is up to 480 kilometers. The 400-volt, 3C charging system can take the battery from 10 to 80 percent in about 20 minutes with compatible DC charging equipment.

The Ultra also carries three XPENG AI Turing chips with a combined claimed computing capacity of 2,250 tera operations per second. Two handle intelligent-driving functions while the third manages the smart cabin.

The L03 runs XPENG’s XOS 6.0 operating system and has a 15.6-inch 2.5K central display, a 26.8-inch head-up display and vehicle-to-load capability.

The X9 is the larger model, a seven-seat electric MPV priced at ₱3.858 million (~$61,700) in Long Range form and ₱4.058 million (~$64,800) with the Second Row Premium Seat Package.

Both versions use a 110-kWh NCM battery and a 235-kW front electric motor producing 450 Nm of torque. XPENG gives the X9 a WLTP range of up to 615 kilometers.

Its 800-volt silicon-carbide platform supports up to 542 kW of DC charging. XPENG says the battery can charge from 10 to 80 percent in about 12 minutes under optimal conditions with suitable charging equipment.

The X9 is more than 5.3 meters long but uses rear-wheel steering to reduce its turning radius to 5.4 meters. It also has dual-chamber air suspension and a powered third row that folds beneath the floor.

The premium package adds two Grand Zero-Gravity second-row seats with 18-way adjustment, powered leg supports and four-way headrests, along with heating, ventilation, memory and 16-point massage. Other equipment includes five-zone climate control, a refrigerator, a 21.4-inch rear entertainment display and a 27-speaker XOPERA sound system.

XPENG is offering different after-sales packages for the two models. X9 buyers receive five years of preventive maintenance and roadside assistance, a five-year vehicle warranty and an eight-year battery and electric-motor warranty, along with a 7-kW wall charger.

L03 buyers receive two years of preventive maintenance, five years of roadside assistance, a five-year vehicle warranty and an eight-year battery and electric-motor warranty. The battery-electric versions include a 7-kW wall charger, while the REEV comes with a 3.5-kW portable charger.

XPENG had initially announced only the range-topping L03 and X9 ahead of the launch. Reservations were set at ₱10,000 (~$160) for the L03 and ₱25,000 (~$400) for the X9. Early buyers were offered ₱10,000 (~$160) in charging credits and an XPENG First Circle Gift Set upon delivery.

Before the launch, country director Katoon Su told Top Gear Philippines that the two models had generated strong interest and that prospective buyers wanted official pricing before making reservations.

The company said it plans to add two more models within six months and expand its network to eight showrooms across Metro Manila, Cebu and Davao by the end of the year. Customer deliveries are expected to begin in the fourth quarter.

The launch also introduced XPENG’s wider technology program. The company displayed its IRON humanoid robot and X2 electric vertical-takeoff-and-landing aircraft alongside the vehicles. The move into robotics and aerial mobility builds on the same AI and computing work used in XPENG’s vehicles. The L03, for example, uses dedicated processors for intelligent-driving and cabin functions.

XPENG Philippines is a direct subsidiary of XPENG and its first subsidiary in Southeast Asia.

data.title: Harvard Study Predicts 32 Percent Of US New Car Sales In US In 2030 Will…
data.description:
A study by the Salata Institute for Climate and Sustainability at Harvard University comes to a rather startling conclusion. Despite all the roadblocks put in the way of the EV revolution by the present US administration, the researchers predict EV sales in the US will quadruple from 8 percent today to 32 percent in 2030.

Absent the headwinds induced by federal policies, that number would have been closer to 48 percent, they claim. While the lower figure is lamentable, it is still an extraordinary prediction, given how legacy US automakers are backpedaling furiously from their prior EV ambitions.

“In the long run, everything’s going in the direction of market-based adoption, despite the moves by the Trump administration that reduce pressure for EV sales,” said Elaine Buckberg, senior fellow at the Salata Institute, one of the report’s authors and a former chief economist for General Motors. The report is entitled “Simulating Impacts of Proposed Trump Policy Changes on Electric Vehicle Adoption” and was released in July. It was written by Buckberg, James Stock, and Cassandra Cole.

The researchers analyzed the impact of several regulatory and legislative steps taken by the government since January 2025, including the revocation of  tax credits for purchase of an electric car and installation of new charging equipment. In addition, the government eliminated restrictions on tailpipe emissions and revoked California’s ability to impose stricter tailpipe emission standards than the federal government requires. Several of these moves are being challenged in court.

Buckberg and team modeled each step and found the one with the biggest impact was removing the EV tax credit, which cut $7,500 off the price of a new electric vehicle. That alone lowered the projected market share of electric cars in 2030 by 6.2 percentage points, the researchers found. Buckberg said the analysis shows the administration’s moves will slow but not stop an expected acceleration in EV adoption, because many prospective buyers would buy the cars even without it.

What will really drive the adoption of electric cars, according to the researchers, are long term changes that will make them more competitive with gasoline vehicles. They suggested the maturation of battery technology will allow automakers to offer EVs with longer range without increasing prices.

In addition, they believe the way people use their electric cars is changing. Because many of the early cars like the first generation Nissan LEAF had limited range — often less than 100 miles — people tended to treat them as second cars for short trips around town. However, since EVs now come with more range, and, because public fast charging options have expanded significantly due to access to the Tesla Supercharger network, they are now being used the same way as conventional cars.

The biggest hurdle to adoption is consumer concern about charging infrastructure, Buckberg said. As that infrastructure grows nationally, gaps in charger coverage will narrow. She suggests making charger status and prices more readily available in charging apps, which would reduce range anxiety and could potentially boost EV sales by as much as 6 percent.

Sharp eyed readers will note that is nearly the same as the percentage reduction caused by the cancellation of the EV purchase tax credit.

“Concerns about charging are the biggest hold back to EV adoption,” Buckberg said. “If we continue to see improvements in battery cost and battery density translating to lower EV prices, when it becomes price equivalent or very close, it becomes much more attractive. If you are doing a road trip, you have at least 300 miles (480 kilometers) of range and can go to a highway charger that takes 10 to 15 minutes, it becomes a more perfect substitute.”

Another advantage of price parity is it could open the eyes of potential buyers to the traditional benefits of electric cars: fast but silent driving, reduced maintenance costs, and freedom from spikes in the cost of gasoline. For those of us who have already made the transition to an EV, regenerative braking is also a big plus we have learned to appreciate.

“The EV tax credit — one of the things that’s gotten the most focus — will become less and less relevant as the price gap narrows,” Buckberg said. “Our research shows that charging is by far the most cost effective lever. Real time data is the least expensive lever of all, and something states can act on right now.”

Is The EV Revolution Over In the US?

Most of us would jump for joy if EV sales amounted to a third of the US new car market by 2030. Yet all the indicators have been flashing red since January 2025. Stellantis no longer seems interested in electric vehicles. Ford has exactly one electric passenger car, which has not been updated significantly since it was introduced nearly seven years ago. GM has more battery electric models than any other US manufacturer, but it is converting its battery factories to making cells for energy storage — not EVs.

Volkswagen was gung ho on its new Scout division, which was supposed to be a showcase for electric vehicles, but its pre-orders have been trending heavily toward a plug-in hybrid version that had been an afterthought. This week, its battery manufacturing arm known as PowerCo announced it will push back the start date of its new factory in St. Thomas, Ontario by two years.

In a statement, Joel Karlsberg, the head of procurement for PowerCo Canada, said, “The St. Thomas gigafactory remains a cornerstone of our North American strategy. We are continuing to build now while determining how and when the facility scales over time. This is about getting the pacing right — not stepping back — to protect our long-term investment, support regional jobs, and position Canada, Ontario, and St. Thomas to benefit in a dynamic and evolving market.”

It is unknown whether the batteries from that factory were intended for Scout vehicles, but Volkswagen currently manufactures no electric cars in North America, having ended production of the ID.4 in Chattanooga earlier this year. Does it sound like the company is putting its plans on hold until the next administration arrives in Washington? It sure seems that way.

GM CEO Mary Barra told Fortune this month she expects EVs to account for 40 to 50 percent of sales by 2030, which is even more optimistic than the Harvard researchers dared to suggest. The company is also moving forward with its “all of the above” propulsion strategy that will include hybrids. So far as we can tell, the Voltec powertrain used in the Chevy Volt will remain locked away in a warehouse, where it has been for nearly a decade. How odd it is that GM refuses to leverage that technology.

Ford is threatening to unleash a new electric midsize pickup truck soon on a platform it says will be the basis of other future electric models. And, not to be outdone, Hyundai says it will focus on extended range electric vehicles that have both a battery and a gasoline engine. The company will also introduce a battery electric version of the Santa Fe soon.

For EVs in the US, it is the best of times; it is the worst of times. Either the future’s so bright we gotta wear shades, or EV drivers will become pariahs pursued by hulking pickup trucks filled with angry people brandishing assault rifles. With that as the background, we have to say the conclusions of the Harvard researchers seem like the best case scenario.

“Full speed ahead, Mister Boatswain. Full speed ahead!”

data.title: Tesla Claims Its Full Self Driving (FSD) Saves Lives, But Wants You To Pay $99/Month…
data.description:
In 2025, an estimated 36,640 traffic fatalities were reported in the US. Let’s dig deeper into auto safety over the years and going forward.

History of seatbelts for safety

  • The first patent for a seatbelt was filed by Edward J. Claghorn in 1885, designed specifically for horse-drawn carriages.
  • Nash was the first American manufacturer to offer seatbelts as an option in 1949.
  • Three-Point Design — Nils Bohlin’s patented three-point seatbelt design in 1959 revolutionized safety, becoming standard in vehicles, starting with the 1959 Volvo. Bohlin felt morally compelled to offer his invention to all automobile manufacturers without cost.
  • All cars sold in the US were required to have seatbelts in 1968.
  • By the 1970s, many countries began enacting laws requiring seatbelt use, significantly reducing fatalities.
  • The latest seatbelts incorporate advanced features such as pretensioners, load limiters, and smart sensors, enhancing passenger safety during collisions.
  • It wasn’t enough to just have seatbelts in all cars. Wearing a seatbelt is now required by law in all US states except New Hampshire.

Air bags for automobile safety

Airbags became mandatory in all new passenger cars sold in the United States starting September 1, 1998, following the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991.

However, even though airbags save lives, they also cause injuries. A few weeks ago, my daughter was in an automobile accident where the airbags deployed. In her case, an airbag shattered her left wrist, causing a compound (bone penetrating the skin) fracture. This illustrates the potential double-edged sword of safety innovations.

The history of seatbelts shows how an innovation that was a novelty at first then became common, then when the saving of lives became apparent, seatbelt use became required.

Where do we stand on safety in the evolution of driving automation like Tesla’s Full Self Driving?

Apr 8, 2026: Elon Musk claimed that Tesla’s “Full Self–Driving” is so much safer than human drivers that it could save 90% of the roughly one million lives lost in car crashes globally.

An embarrassing personal story: On June 9, I was driving my 2018 Tesla Model 3 in Madison, Wisconsin, using Full Self Driving. At an intersection, I over-road FSD and ran a stop sign. I was struck in the rear of my car by a woman who wasn’t paying close attention and was crossing the intersection in a perpendicular way. I am certain that if I had let FSD drive the car, we would have stopped at the stop sign and the accident would have been avoided. Fortunately, my wife and I were not injured and neither was the woman driving the other car. The woman in the other car was probably saved from injury by her seatbelt.

FSD doesn’t use alcohol or drugs, it doesn’t text, and it doesn’t fall asleep. If you also speculate on how often drivers don’t pay close attention for many reasons and how often they make bad decisions while driving, it doesn’t take much speculation to imagine how often accidents could be avoided by FSD. See Waymo’s recent news as well for more on this topic.

On the other hand, there have been numerous reports of Tesla FSD causing accidents, and we don’t have full, public data on this matter.

Tesla is not only charging $99/month for its certainly lifesaving FSD technology, but it removed a potentially lifesaving technology (automatic lane centering) as a standard feature from all of its new cars a few months ago. Motivation: get more people to pay $99/month for FSD.

How is this morally defensible? Tesla has probably spent billions of dollars developing FSD up to this point. Tesla has a large team of engineers working to improve FSD and continues to train it on billions of traffic situations on a huge supercomputer. Tesla has also installed upgraded cameras and upgraded computers that enable the running of the latest version of FSD V14 in all of its new cars since mid 2023. FSD is not perfect now and it makes some sense for Tesla to have a money stream coming in so that it can continue to afford to improve it. But is this worth the price of more traffic fatalities now?

It could be quite like the seatbelt story of the past, which went from novelty to a sophisticated, proven, required feature in all cars. We are probably still in the novelty stage at this point with automatic driving systems. In fact, automatic driving systems are much more complex than seatbelts. Tesla’s proprietary FSD is arguably by far the most comprehensive, best performing automatic driving system that works everywhere in the United States today.

Tesla’s FSD is not perfect, but it doesn’t have to be. It just must be significantly safer than human drivers to save some of the now ~370,000 people who are being killed in traffic accidents in the US every year. I have been driving my 2026 Tesla Model Y with FSD V14 for 4 months now. Tesla is required to call it “FSD Supervised” because it’s not perfect. It still makes mistakes, for example, on lane selection at stoplights and with the beginning and end (parking) of trips. There is infinite speculation about when (if ever) it will be good enough to remove the “Supervised” qualifier. When will it be good enough that you can text, read a book, and go to sleep when driving? When will you be able to send your car to pick up the kids at school? Tesla has a huge team of engineers training FSD with billions of traffic situations on a huge supercomputer working to reach that next level.

However, from my experience, FSD V14 is darn good already! It has been perfect for me on the highways. I speculate that it will be good enough to eliminate the “supervised” qualification on highways in time for the next version (V15).

Have we reached the point where Tesla will be morally required to make sure that all new Teslas come with FSD as standard equipment, and will it be morally required to install the software on all Teslas that have the hardware capable of running the latest version of FSD? When will the company be morally obligated to offer FSD for free to any manufacturer willing to install the necessary hardware to run the FSD system? (Much as Nils Bohlin did with his patented 3-point seat belt design in 1959.) Tesla’s proprietary Superchargers were a huge step forward that made driving an EV cross-country practical in the US for the first time. Not many months ago, Tesla made its Superchargers available to all other manufacturers for the first time. Superchargers are now called North American Charging Standard (NACS) chargers, and they have truly become the North American standard for chargers. Are we not far from the time when FSD will be the universally adopted automatic driving standard in the US? Once again, the situation is not as simple as seatbelts. Other manufactures think that Tesla’s all-camera system will never be a good as systems employing lidar and radar as well. This will certainly be true for very bad weather. However, Tesla’s system seems much more economical to deploy and may be good enough. After all, human drivers also pull off the road in extremely bad weather.

data.title: Waymo — Nearly 1,000 Avoided Injuries
data.description:
Waymo has published another update on the safety benefits of its robotaxi service. The company says it has now logged more than 300 human lifetimes of driving, and that the safety benefits are clear already.

Across Waymo’s 270 million miles of fully autonomous driving, the company says that injuries to at least 841 people have been completely avoided. Because Waymo robotaxis drive better than human drivers (on average).

This is notable, but what caught my eye even more is that this number was up significantly from 544 avoided injuries just in December. The number of avoided human injuries has been growing exponentially, as we can see in the following chart.

Waymo provides more info: “Our latest analysis of the Waymo Driver’s safety performance now covers over 270 million miles of fully autonomous operations through the end of June 2026 — the distance equivalent of driving the length of Route 66 over 110,000 times. This safety data includes analysis of five of our major metropolitan service areas: Atlanta, Austin, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and San Francisco.

“Across these cities, the Waymo Driver continues to outperform human benchmarks. Regardless of fault, it was involved in 841 fewer injury-causing crashes — an 82% reduction compared to human drivers. When it comes to more severe collisions, the impact is even more pronounced: the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) serious injury or worse crashes than humans.”

An 82% reduction in injuries! And a 95% reduction for serious injuries!! That’s dramatic improvement. At this point, one could argue there should be subsidies for such service in order to protect more humans. Though, of course, it’s best of there’s a strong business case for the service and it can grow organically and exponentially.

“The safety impact extends directly to where road users are most exposed. Whether it’s riding in a bike lane alongside the vehicle, stepping into a crosswalk at dusk, or navigating dense traffic on a motorcycle, the Waymo Driver significantly reduces risk — cutting injury-causing crashes involving pedestrians by 93%, cyclists by 86%, and motorcyclists by 82%,” Waymo adds.

“View the full data and methodology here. The Waymo Driver also undergoes a formal safety review before deployment on public roads. You can see the acceptance criteria used to evaluate its readiness in this paper.”

Dive into the data if you want, and feel to share anything you notice and find important in there as well. Perhaps I’ll spend some of the weekend looking into it further myself.

data.title: How to Become Clean Energy Evangelist
data.description:
A few weeks ago, CleanTechnica published my Clean Energy Evangelist Report Card. However, 1) I left some things out which I will add here and in a future article. 2) Please see some suggestions on how YOU can be a Clean Energy Evangelist.

If you are going to be a clean energy evangelist, you need to: 1) Be knowledgeable on what’s most important, 2) Be knowledgeable on what the advantage and cost differential of each clean energy choice is, 3) Set an example by making as many clean energy choices in your life as possible. Unless you have unlimited funds, you can’t run out and reduce your fossil fuel use to zero immediately. However, when it’s time to junk your old car or if your water heater, furnace, or lawnmower quits on you, that’s the time to seriously consider a clean energy replacement. Hopefully you can eventually switch everything you own to battery electric and heat pump electric, install solar panels on your roof, and install battery storage in your garage. Also, carpool and use public transportation when you can.

A real clean energy evangelist will take his EV to car shows (see lead photo) and drives it in parades. I’ve done this for 10 years, but I was more successful in the beginning. At that time, I was able to get friends with EVs to join me. Lately I can’t get friends and family to help and I’m doing it by myself. If you look carefully, in the photo you can see my 100% Electric and 100% Automatic Driving placards on my windows. At the car show this summer, very few people were interested in my brand new 2026 Tesla Model Y. The show was populated with gas motorheads showing off their restored gasmobiles like the old red ford truck you see in the photo. I won’t do this again unless I can find someone with a more unusual EV like a Rivian truck to join me. However, I will still do the 4th of July parade.

The most important thing you can do to be a clean energy evangelist is to replace your gas vehicle with a pure battery electric vehicle. Driving a BEV is a visible statement that everyone around you will observe. If there are few EVs in your area, it’s important that people know that an EV is a practical alternative to a gas car. Seeing yours will help accomplish this. Your present gas car burns more fossil-fuel-producing CO2 (than is burned producing the electricity to run your EV that replaces it), emits more lung dangerous sub-micron particles, and produces more sub-micron particles from brake pad wear than anything else you do. A BEV doesn’t burn any fossil fuel while operating, is 90% efficient, and seldom uses its brakes. Everyone knows that my Tesla is a BEV, but when I drove another BEV brand, I had small silver 100% Electric stickers made and I put them on the front and back of the car as you see in the photo below.

sMy Tesla 2026 base Model Y rear wheel drive with mountain ebike. Pine Isle. Medicine Lake. Three Lakes, Wisconsin. August 10, 2026. Fritz Hasler photo.If you are buying a new Tesla base Model Y (see above), you can get a loan now with 1.5% interest (up from 0% thee month months ago when I bought mine) with monthly payments of ~$559. A base Model 3 got 2% interest with payments of $529/month. There is a new long-wheelbase three-row 6 seat Model YL launch edition which just became available for $992/month. With interest rates higher now, these rates are very attractive. All new Teslas have Hardware V4 that can run “Full Self Driving” V14 for $99/month. All new Teslas have an EPA battery range of over 300 miles. Those on a smaller budget can get a used Tesla for much less. A year ago, my son bought a gorgeous 7-year-old Tesla Model 3 Performance (see below) with good range and warrantee still left on the battery for $15,000.

One problem with buying a used EV is that most used car lots don’t know how to sell EVs. They don’t know what they have and don’t know how to catigorize them and communicate that information to their customers. They don’t know how much range the EV has left on the battery, whether a Tesla is dual or single motor, Tesla Hardware 2, 3 or 4. or whether it comes with a permanent Full Self Driving subscription. They don’t know if they have one of the golden few Teslas sold between mid 2023 and spring 2026 that come with HW 4 and a permanent FSD V14 subscription. Permanent FSD subscriptions are no longer available. You usually have to go to the lot and get in the car to find out this information. One advantage: Since they don’t know what they’ve got, you could possibly steal a deal.

All US EV brands can now charge at most (all newer) Tesla Superchargers, and some even have native Tesla sockets that don’t require an adapter. A Chevy Bolt EV starts at $27,600 and comes with a native NACS (Tesla) socket.

Buying an ebike is your bookend transportation action. In my case, my ebike substitutes for the second car that my wife and I no longer own. Get an ebike like the one shown above, or better yet, a mountain ebike like the ones shown below. A mountain ebike can drive on gravel if needed and can be driven off the edge of the road in an emergency. It also gives a smoother ride on any kinds of bumps in the road and can drop off and jump curbs if needed. I frequently go on errands on my ebike, especially when my wife is driving our Tesla. I pick up prescriptions, go to the gym, or pick up an item or two at the grocery store. With an ebike, you can make longer trips and climb hills much more easily. If you are not athletically able to ride a two-wheeler, an electric trike or 3-wheel recumbent bike will serve.

One thing I left out of my previous article:

  • Switch out your house to 100% LED light bulbs. Maybe most of you did this long ago, but I keep finding incandescent and fluorescent bulbs that I missed. Several years ago, I switched almost every bulb in my two houses and garage to fluorescents. More recently, when IKEA ran a fabulous special on LED bulbs, I bought 200 60-watt equivalents and threw out all the fluorescents in my Utah house, my Wisconsin house, and my Wisconsin house garage. A fluorescent bulb uses 25% of the energy of an incandescent bulb with the same light output. An LED bulb uses 10% of the energy of an incandescent bulb with the same light output. You get a double bonus here because they save you 90% of the money you used to spend on lighting…. And the LEDs last longer. They are supposed to last 20 years. I’m 86, so, in principle, I should never have to change light bulbs again. This has not been the case in practice. Maybe some of my LEDs may last 20 years, but I have had to change quite a few. When IKEA ran its 60W-equivalent LED sale years ago, I think I paid 50 cents a bulb. Unfortunately, they cost ~$2.50 at IKEA now. However, you can buy 60W-equivalent LEDs online at Amazon for $1.28 each. Saving 90% on electricity, you will pay back the installation cost very quickly, and with longer-life LEDs, this is a monetary and convenience win, win, win over time. Recently, I found a hidden 2-ft fluorescent tube bulb in a closet that had burned out. When I went to replace it, I discovered ACE Hardware no longer stocks fluorescent tube bulbs, so I came home with an LED.

I will discuss some other items in another article, e.g.:

  • Switch your fossil gas or resistance electric water heater to a heat pump water heater.
  • Switch your fossil gas furnace or resistance electric heating to heat pump heating.

data.title: Uruguay EV Sales Report: Sales Soar in August as Market Share Reaches 56%!
data.description:
Latin America’s small champion keeps making headlines and surpassing even the most optimistic expectations. Uruguay’s EV adoption has diverged from the region and reached a level that many of us would’ve though irrationally optimist only two years ago.

Amidst a booming vehicle market, Uruguay EV sales have exploded through 2026, reaching record levels in six out of the eight months this year. The result has been a market that in record time has gone from early adopter to majority adopter, going from 5% to 50% BEV market share in only two and a half years!

Let’s look at the numbers!

Market overview

EV sales in August grew by an impressive 171% YoY, getting very close to 4,000 units and even surpassing the previous records, set in July, by 22%.

Since Uruguay started providing data on PHEV sales, we’ve been able to add them to our tally, but they remain very limited, representing only around 1/10th of total EV sales. Uruguay, like most other small markets in the region, remains a highly BEV-centric one.

And now we get to the most interesting part: market share. Thanks to impressive growth, EVs now account for 56% of total vehicle sales in Uruguay, 51% of these being BEVs, meaning one in every two cars sold in Uruguay in August had a fully electric powertrain!

As a result, we’re seeing combustion-based powertrains (ICEV+HEV) melt away — despite a strong market (sales in the vehicle market grew by 16% in Jan–Aug 2026 compared to the same period in 2025), fuel-based cars have now fallen 16% throughout the year, and 20% compared to 2024.

Looking at sales per brand, the market remains balanced in August, with former uber-leader BYD still in first place, but with “only” 25% of the market, followed by Geely and GAC. It’s important to mention that Tesla is yet to start deliveries, so despite the very competitive pricing it has announces, it’s still not a part of the competition.

Model-wise, Uruguay is yet another country where the Geely Geome/EX2 has managed to win first prize, surpassing the BYD Seagull (now second) and the GAC Aion UT, a very interesting and competitive model that we seldom see on our podiums.

Year to date, BYD remains the leader, followed by Geely and Dongfeng on the podium, and then followed by GAC in fourth place and Chevrolet in fifth place. The US brand is the only legacy automaker capable of making it into the top 10 thanks to its rebranded Baojun Yep Plus Spark EUV and Wuling Starlight S Captiva EV.

Model-wise, we find BYD getting gold and silver thanks to the success of the Yuan Up (now including a PHEV version) and the Seagull, followed by the value-for-money Dongfeng Nammi. In fourth place rests the Geely EX2 (a surprisingly good result if we take into account that it only arrived in the country very recently), and in fifth place the Spark EUV.

A matter of context

Uruguay’s explosive growth in EV adoption is quite baffling. Even though there are clear economic incentives for it — mainly, the most expensive gasoline on the continent — the fact remains that fuel prices have barely grown due to Trump’s war on Iran (with only an 11–13% increase since September 2023), meaning this factor, though important, is probably not what’s driving such growth in the short term.

More important could be the announcement of new taxes for EVs from 2027: the Uruguayan government has stated it will start to charge a 5% internal tax on EVs imported at a price between USD$19,001 and $27,000, and 9% for those above $27,001. Though symbolically important, the fact is this tax remains quite low, far below what ICEVs pay (which can go up to 35%), and cheaper EVs will remain exempt.

Regardless, the announcement of taxes by itself could motivate a lot of people to jump the gun and get an EV at pre-tax prices — but since prices will not go up substantially, I doubt that we will see a significant reduction in sales in 2028. Though, growth will for sure go down. After all, you cannot sustain >100% rates of growth when you’re already above 50% market share.

But my opinion on Uruguay’s EV sales is simple: the country has found that EVs provide better value, and the population is acting on this basic fact. As time goes on, we will see this in more and more countries in the region.

Final thoughts

Uruguay’s record EV sales, and specifically BEV sales, put the country on par with global leaders, below Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Ethiopia, and Nepal, but above China(!), the Netherlands, Belgium, and the UK.

But more important than that, we’re seeing firsthand how fast things can change due mainly to EVs becoming a better option than the alternative. As a result, ICEV sales are now falling, with fleet numbers soon to follow in the coming years. Uruguay is only the first domino to fall, and soon we could see similar results all over the region.

One last thing: all this growth is happening before Tesla starts deliveries, and even if the Uruguayan market is already very competitive, we saw in Colombia that having access to a Tesla at $30,000 or less can have quite an impact.

So, what do our readers think? How long before fuel-based cars in Uruguay fall consistently below 20%? Six months? A year? Two years? Please do let us know your comments below.
